item.title: Earnings macro week ahead: The Fed and Big Tech report on the same day
item.description:
The Fed decision is Wednesday, October 28, but markets have mostly given up on a move: fed funds futures put the odds of a hold at roughly 90-92%. The market believes that a hike less than a week before the midterms would be politically awkward. So now the question isn’t really about a rate hike in the week ahead but December and that is now at 85% for a hike.

I will be watching macro data including Thursday's PCE report but I will also be looking for macro signals from companies reporting this week. Last week, we heard from airlines that continued to highlight strong travel demand and corporate spending in a good economic sign, but what abotut the rest of the economy? Housing is particularly interesting with interest rates high and a deep, ongoing recession in that sector.

Monday, Oct 26

After market:Nucor is the best steel commentary in the business. Watch what management says about nonresidential construction and order books as long rates push higher. Steel priced have been moving up but that's more about tariffs than macro. Public Storage is an underrated housing tell: people move into storage when they move house, and nobody is moving with 7% mortgages. Welltower and Sun Communities show rate-sensitive real estate with 30-year mortgages above 7%.

Tuesday, Oct 27 — FOMC day one

Before market:UPS is the trade and freight read: parcel volumes, tariff effects and the small-business shipper. Coca-Cola gives global volumes and pricing, plus FX drag from the strong dollar. Sherwin-Williams is a major housing tell, since repaint demand tracks existing home sales. Hilton reports RevPAR, the cleanest gauge of business travel demand. Royal Caribbean shows discretionary spending with fuel costs biting, though note that Carnival jumped on earnings early in October.

After market:Visa is the macro report of the day. Payment volumes are a real-time spending series, and cross-border shows travel demand. Keep in mind that nominal growth flatters volumes when CPI is at 3.7%.

Wednesday, Oct 28 — Fed decision at 2 pm ET

Before market:ADP is the most underrated macro report on the calendar. Its client pays-per-control numbers are effectively a payroll survey. Any slowing in hiring at small and mid-sized businesses would land hours before Warsh speaks. GE Vernova is the power-equipment trade: gas turbine backlog, pricing and data center demand. That's a big macro driver right now and we will see how bullish they are on the order book.   Phillips 66 reports refining margins as the Iran war makes for extreme profitability.

After market: The Fed statement and press conference will barely be digested before Microsoft and Alphabet report. Their capex now shows up in GDP, so watch whether AI spending guidance is still rising at ramping borrowing costs. Alphabet’s search ads are a broad read on the ad economy. Chipotle is the middle-income consumer; and something of an inflation battleground.

Thursday, Oct 29 — September PCE

Before market:Caterpillar is the industrial report of the week. It covers construction, mining, power generation for data centers and dealer inventories in one place. It's been a standout AI winner but a volatile name. Mastercard confirms or contradicts Visa.

After market:Amazon is two macro reads in one: retail volumes show the consumer and AWS capex shows AI spending. Starbucks shows discretionary traffic and China. Mondelez covers cocoa costs and pricing tolerance. Coinbase and Strategy are risk-appetite gauges. Intel and Sandisk cover the PC and storage cycle and those ones will surely be big market movers. 

Friday, Oct 30

Before market:CN is the one I’d watch from a Canadian perspective. Rail volumes are a direct read on Canadian trade flows, tariff damage and the resource economy. Chevron and BP show how the majors are allocating capex with the Middle East premium in oil. I'll look for signs on drilling discipline.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US expected to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian products as soon as today - report
item.description:
Election season is doing what trade negotiators couldn’t.

The Wall Street Journal reports the US is preparing to lift 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products, with a proclamation possibly coming as soon as today. The motivation is political: Maine Sen. Susan Collins has been lobbying for relief and is in a dead heat with Democrat Troy Jackson with less than two weeks to go until Election Day.

Unfortunately, there is no real sign of a political thaw here as Trump could also raise other tariffs. USD/CAD is dow n18 pips to 1.3990 today and unmoved on this report.

The details:

  • Scope and timing could still change, according to the WSJ’s sources
  • The cuts may be offset by higher tariffs on other Canadian goods
  • The White House says any announcement will come from the administration and calls the reports speculation
  • USTR declined to comment

This would be the second adjustment to the 50% tariffs. Last month, Washington exempted road salt and cement and added other products to keep the affected total at about $20 billion, or roughly 5% of Canadian exports to the US. Collins took credit for that change on the campaign trail. Jackson’s reply in their debate was that Mainers “can’t eat road salt.” Food and lumber are a different matter.

The politics go well beyond Maine. In Michigan, GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers is now running ads urging Trump to end the trade war with Canada after spending months backing it. In New Hampshire, John Sununu has also criticized the Canada tariffs.

For background, Trump imposed the 50% levies in late August after last-minute talks broke down. He used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the Smoot-Hawley provision, which had never been used before. Canada retaliated, Trump responded with import bans on some Canadian products, and he has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian autos in January if there’s no deal. A New Jersey food importer filed suit this week arguing Section 338 goes beyond the administration’s authority.

Again, I don't see this as a thaw. It’s a swap and the dollar value covered stays around $20 billion and the headline effect for Canada is mostly reshuffling. At the same time, if he wanted real political gains for Republicans before the midterms, he could drop the tariffs altogether and make a deal.

Update: The announcement came from Collins, who noted several products: blueberry, potoatos, apple and seaweed among them.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Baker Hughes US oil rig count rises 1 to 460. Total rigs unchanged at 603
item.description:
Baker Hughes reports that the US oil rig count rose by 1 to 460 in the week ending October 23. Gas rigs fell by 1 to 132, offsetting the increase and leaving the total US rig count unchanged at 603.

The US breakdown, including year-ago comparisons:

  • Oil rigs: 460 versus 459 last week and 420 a year ago. Up 40 year over year.

  • Gas rigs: 132 versus 133 last week and 121 a year ago. Up 11 year over year.

  • Miscellaneous rigs: Unchanged at 11 versus 9 a year ago.

  • Total US rigs: Unchanged at 603 versus 550 a year ago. Up 53, or 9.6%, year over year.

In Canada, the rig count increased by 3 to 220, compared with 199 a year ago. That brought the combined North American count to 823, up 3 on the week and up 74 from 749 a year ago.

The weekly changes are modest, but the year-over-year comparison shows a higher level of drilling activity, with oil rigs accounting for most of the US increase.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Biggest earnings week ahead: Can Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon turn the Nasdaq tide? Or will the ships sink?
item.description:
The biggest earnings week ahead comes at an important time for the US stock market. The Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 are both trading below their respective 100-day moving averages, putting the sellers more in control from a technical perspective. Next week’s calendar brings Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, along with a broad mix of semiconductor, industrial, consumer and energy companies. The question is straightforward: Can earnings and guidance give buyers a reason to step back in, or will the results open the door for another shove lower?

The technical backdrop: Buyers have work to do

The technology-heavy indices head into the week with their 100-day moving averages overhead and their 200-day moving averages looming below:

  • Nasdaq Composite: Trading near 26,022, below its 100-day moving average at 26,255. The 200-day moving average is at 24,922, about 4.23% below the current price.

  • Nasdaq 100: Trading near 29,037, below its 100-day moving average at 29,573. Its 200-day moving average is at 27,836, about 4.14%% below the current price.

For buyers, the first step is to get back above those 100-day moving averages and stay above. That would take some of the pressure off and give traders something positive to lean against.

Absent that, rallies can still be corrections within a more bearish technical picture. The 200-day moving averages become increasingly important downside targets if the selling continues. They are not guaranteed destinations, but traders need to know where they are.

Wednesday and Thursday bring the heavyweights

Wednesday after the close is a key event, with Microsoft and Alphabet reporting alongside ServiceNow, KLA and other widely followed names.

For Microsoft, the focus will be on Azure cloud growth, demand for AI services, and whether the spending needed to build that business is translating into revenue and profits. For Alphabet, traders will watch search advertising, Google Cloud, and how AI is affecting both the opportunity and the cost of doing business.

Amazon follows Thursday after the close. AWS cloud growth, retail margins and its own investment spending will help shape the market’s assessment of the technology outlook.

The common thread? Investors will want evidence that spending is producing results—and guidance that supports more growth ahead.

The key releases for the week. 

Monday, October 26

  • Before the open: Verizon.

  • After the close: Celestica, Cadence Design Systems, Rambus, and Whirlpool.

Celestica, Cadence, Rambus and Whirlpool get the week started with a look across technology infrastructure and the semiconductor supply chain.

Tuesday, October 27

  • Before the open: SoFi, UPS, Coca-Cola, Corning, Freeport-McMoRan, PayPal and S&P Global.

  • After the close: Robinhood, Seagate, Visa, and Waste Management.

UPS provides a read on shipping activity, while Visa and PayPal offer insight into payment volumes and consumer spending. Robinhood adds a look at retail trading activity.

Wednesday, October 28

  • Before the open: Amphenol, Boston Scientific, Vertiv, GE Vernova, UBS, ADP and Phillips 66.

  • After the close:Microsoft, Alphabet, ServiceNow, KLA, Carvana, FedEx, Fortinet, T-Mobile and Chipotle.

This is a particularly busy day. Vertiv, Amphenol and GE Vernova bring infrastructure and power demand into focus before the technology heavyweights (Microsoft and Alphabet) report after the close.

Thursday, October 29

  • Before the open: Caterpillar, Carrier, Eli Lilly, Vulcan Materials, STMicroelectronics and L3Harris.

  • After the close:Amazon, Intel, Sandisk, Roblox, Reddit, Twilio, Coinbase, Starbucks and Rivian.

Caterpillar offers a window into equipment demand and business investment. After the close, Amazon leads a wide-ranging group covering chips, consumer spending, digital advertising and cryptocurrency trading.

Friday, October 30

  • Before the open: Exxon Mobil, Chevron, BP, Regeneron, AstraZeneca, and General Dynamics.

Energy takes a prominent role to finish the week, with traders watching production, margins, spending plans and management’s outlook.

Watch the reaction as closely as the results

An earnings beat does not automatically mean a stock moves higher. Expectations matter. Guidance matters. So does what has already been priced in (watch the technicals for clues on what is priced in).

If companies deliver good numbers and their shares cannot rally—or an early rally quickly fades—that tells traders something about the appetite to buy. Conversely, disappointing results followed by a recovery can signal that sellers had their shot and could not keep control.

For the broader technology market, the technical roadmap is clear. Get above the 100-day moving averages and stay above, and the buyers improve their position. Stay below, and the sellers retain the advantage, with the 200-day moving averages waiting underneath.

The earnings will provide the headlines. The price action will tell us what traders think of them.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stocks post weekly losses. French yields climb. Brent above $117/crude above $103
item.description:
As London/European traders head home for the weekend, the major European stock indices are closing mixed for the day, but lower across the board for the week. Spain and Italy managed gains today. Germany, France and the UK finished lower.

The closing numbers and weekly changes show:

  • German DAX: 25,152.30, down 0.86% today and 1.84% for the week
  • France’s CAC 40: 7,782.83, down 0.36% today and 2.19% for the week
  • UK FTSE 100: 10,690.37, down 0.32% today and 1.76% for the week
  • Spain’s IBEX 35: 18,989.81, up 0.40% today, but down 1.74% for the week
  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 48,558.85, up 0.36% today, but down 2.60% for the week

Italy’s bounce today helped, but it still finished with the largest weekly decline of the five markets.

Market breadth also showed the uneven nature of today’s session. Germany had 24 decliners versus 14 advancers, France had 24 versus 16, and the UK had 53 versus 38. Spain and Italy had more stocks rising than falling, supporting their positive closes.

French bonds stand out for the week

The European bond market told a more divided story. German and UK 10-year yields moved lower for the week, while France and Italy moved higher. Spain was unchanged. French yields moved higher this week as budget gridlock, a large deficit and worsening protests raised doubts about the government’s ability to control its debt. Investors demanded a higher return to hold French bonds, with the risk of a Moody’s credit-rating downgrade adding to the pressure. The benchmark 10 year yield in France is at the highest level since 2002.

The weekly changes in benchmark 10-year yields were:

  • Germany: Down 7.4 basis points
  • France: Up 16.7 basis points
  • UK: Down 3.8 basis points
  • Spain:Unchanged
  • Italy: Up 7.0 basis points

France remains the standout. Its 10-year yield fell 6.2 basis points today to 5.018%, providing some relief, but that did little to reverse the weekly increase.

With German yields falling and French yields rising, the French premium over Germany widened by 24.1 basis points this week. That is a sizable divergence. French bonds underperformed even as German bonds attracted buying.

Elsewhere today, Germany’s 10-year yield rose 1.4 basis points to 3.346%, the UK yield rose 2.7 basis points to 5.361%, Spain edged up 0.2 basis points to 4.046%, and Italy slipped 0.2 basis points to 4.580%.

US stocks are mixed as Treasury yields rebound

In the US, technology shares are showing some recovery after yesterday’s selling, but the gains are not carrying the whole market higher. The Dow is lower by nearly 500 points, and the S&P 500 is also modestly lower.

At the snapshot:

  • Dow industrial average: 52,387.25, down 486.03 points or 0.92%
  • S&P 500: 7,653.87, down 9.56 points or 0.12%
  • Nasdaq Composite: 26,077.58, up 68.72 points or 0.26%
  • Nasdaq 100: 29,117.39, up 158.71 points or 0.55%
  • Russell 2000: 2,777.65, down 6.38 points or 0.23%

The Nasdaq indices are getting a bounce, but the Dow and small caps are lagging. Buyers are having a shot at stabilizing technology shares. The broader market still has work to do. See the video and post on the technicals driving the major indices HERE.

US Treasury yields are moving higher, with the largest increases at the shorter end of the curve:

  • 2-year:4.6946%, up 6.0 basis points
  • 5-year:4.8120%, up 4.4 basis points
  • 10-year:4.9904%, up 3.7 basis points
  • 30-year:5.3114%, up 2.4 basis points

The US 10-year yield is back within a basis point of 5%.

Oil jumps above $103. Gold and silver retreat

Crude oil is the standout commodity move. The quoted contract is trading at $103.03, up $3.56 or 3.58%. The move puts oil firmly above the $100 level and keeps energy costs in focus as bond yields rebound. Brent Crude is above $117.  

Gold, meanwhile, is trading near an important round number at $4,003.03, down $21.48 or 0.53%. Silver is also lower, down 0.87% to $54.10. Both metals are retreating as US yields move higher.

Bitcoin is firmer at $81,532, up $2,160 or 2.72%, while natural gas is up 1.97% at $6.524.

The week ends with losses across the major European equity markets, a sharp widening in France’s yield premium over Germany, and oil above $103. Today’s gains in Spain, Italy and US technology shares offer some relief, but the buying remains selective.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks are mixed, but weak breadth keeps the recovery in question
item.description:
The four major US stock indices are telling different stories today. The Dow industrial average is under the most pressure, the S&P 500 is modestly lower, and the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 are trading higher.

Here is the snapshot:

  • Dow industrial average: Down 473.64 points, or 0.90%, at 52,394.34.

  • S&P 500: Down 10.18 points, or 0.13%, at 7,653.25.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Up 57.33 points, or 0.22%, at 26,066.19.

  • Nasdaq 100: Up 133.19 points, or 0.46%, at 29,091.88.

However, look underneath those headline numbers and the picture is less encouraging. Declining stocks outnumber advancing stocks across all four indices—even in the two Nasdaq indices that are trading higher.

Within the Dow, just five stocks are higher versus 25 lower. In the S&P 500, there are 147 advancers versus 336 decliners. The Nasdaq 100 has 44 stocks advancing versus 56 declining, while the Nasdaq Composite has 1,183 advancers versus 1,827 decliners.

That tells traders the buying is selective. The Nasdaq indices are getting enough support from their more influential stocks to keep the headline readings positive, but the gains are not being shared across the market.

The sector breadth reinforces that caution. Energy stands out with 19 stocks advancing and just one declining. Technology is more balanced at 28 versus 26. Financials, healthcare, industrials and utilities all show considerably more decliners than advancers.

So what does that mean for traders?

The positive Nasdaq readings give buyers something to work with. But can they build on those gains? Can the S&P turn higher and the Dow find support? Or will the weak breadth eventually drag the Nasdaq indices back down?

For me, the technicals help define those answers. A bounce is a start. Getting above resistance—and staying above—is what gives buyers more control. Hold below those levels, and sellers can still lean against them.

In the video, I take a look at the Dow industrial average, S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100, outlining the key technical levels in play, why they matter, and what buyers and sellers need to do next.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUDUSD recovery runs into the 100-day moving average. What next?
item.description:
The AUDUSD has found support and resistance against two separate moving averages. They are providing the borderlines for both buyers and sellers now. 

The low for the week was on Monday.

Recall, that the AUDUSD has worked its way higher from Monday’s low near 0.6970, with buyers pushing back above a familiar swing area between 0.6989 and 0.6994.

That area is marked by the red numbered circles on the chart. The repeated highs and reactions tell traders why it matters. What had been a ceiling needed to be broken to give the buyers more control. Once above, that ceiling becomes a potential floor.

The break higher opened the door for a move toward the next key target: the 100-day moving average at 0.7032.

The buyers made their move. But at that moving average, the sellers showed up.

Sellers lean against the 100-day MA

On Wednesday, the price tested the 100-day moving average and stalled. Today, sellers leaned against that level again.

Why sell there? It gives traders a clear level to define and limit risk. Stay below, and the sellers can look for a rotation lower. Move above and stay above, and that bearish trade loses some of its technical support.

A sustained break above 0.7032 would have traders looking toward:

  • 0.70447: An intervening chart level.

  • 0.70506: The 200-day moving average.

  • 0.70654: The 50% midpoint of the September-to-October decline.

Getting above the 100-day MA would be another step forward for the buyers. They would still have work to do, however, with the 200-day MA waiting above.

Buyers defend the 100-hour MA below

While sellers have defended resistance, buyers have also been leaning against support.

Pullbacks on Thursday and Friday stalled near the 100-hour moving average, currently around 0.7008. That makes it a close risk-defining level for buyers looking for the recovery to continue.

Stay above is more bullish. Break below, and the door opens for a rotation back toward:

  • 0.6989–0.6994: The swing area marked by the red numbered circles.

  • 0.6984: The rising 200-hour moving average.

A move back below those levels would take away more of the buyers’ progress from earlier this week.

For now, the battle is defined. Sellers are leaning against the 100-day MA above. Buyers are leaning against the 100-hour MA below. Traders are waiting for the next shove.

In the video, I walk through those levels, explain why they matter, and outline what buyers and sellers need to do to take more control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why the market senses a weekend Iran escalation and what happens next
item.description:
Brent prices are above $116 and more than 2.5% on the day as the market sniffs out a weekend attack on Iran.

The war hasn't gone to Trump's plan and Republican polling and approval numbers are dismal. In addition, Israeli PM Netanyahu is unlikely to remain Prime Minister after Tuesday's vote (odds around 30% of him remaining PM). 

Trump himself outlined the playbook 14 years ago:

The reports seem to indicate this will be a short-lived attacked perhaps aimed at pickaxe mountain and some missile sites. My best guess is that Trump attacks and then tries to declare victory early next week in order to reset the talking points in a deeply unpopular war. The problem is that oil prices aren't exactly cooperating at the moment and that's a tough sell.

The big complication is that we don't know what Iran has in reserve and how far it will go in retaliation. There were all kinds of warnings this week about cutting subsea cables, attacking data centers, attacking US bases in the region and attacking gulf energy infrastructure. US attacks might cross that line and result in the escalation spiral we've been in for awhile.

What makes me a bit more optimistic is that this attack appears to be leaking. That means it's leaking to Iran too, or could have even been telegraphed. In short, it could all be for show, like so many of the Iran-Israel attacks in the prior few years.

Brent daily:

In any case, all of this is speculation. We've learned from Trump this year that there really isn't a plan, it's just all improvisation and the analysis doesn't need to go any deeper than his tweet from 14 years ago. His aim -- if he attacks -- is likely to simply reshuffle the deck and try to find a way out of a quagmire.

In better news for oil bears, a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia and the US is planned for early November. The tone from Zelensky in the past few days appears to have changed and maybe there's an opening for peace.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: UMich final October final consumer sentiment 48.0 vs 46.3 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 46.3
  • Prelim was 48.1
  • Current conditions 46.7 vs 50.9 prior
  • Expectations 48.4 vs 46.3 prior
  • 1-year inflation 4.7% vs 4.7% prior
  • 5 -year inflation 3.5% vs 3.5% prior

This indicator is near all-time lows but in the last number of years it's morphed into more of a political indicator than a spending one. The Fed still watches the inflation numbers though.

The University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers produces one of the oldest and most widely followed gauges of US household sentiment. Results come out twice a month, both at 10 am ET: a preliminary reading around mid-month and a final reading near the end of the month that incorporates the full sample. Revisions between the two are usually modest, but they occasionally shift the picture, particularly on inflation expectations.

The headline Index of Consumer Sentiment is built from questions about personal finances, business conditions and buying conditions for big-ticket items. It’s indexed to 100 in early 1966. The survey splits into two sub-indexes, current economic conditions and consumer expectations, with the expectations measure feeding into the Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index.

The inflation expectations figures are often the most market-relevant part of the report. Respondents estimate price changes over the next year and over the next five to 10 years. The Federal Reserve watches the longer-run measure closely as a gauge of whether inflation expectations are becoming unanchored, and a jump in either can move Treasury yields and rate pricing.

The survey moved from telephone interviews to an online format in 2024, which has made comparisons with older data trickier. Readings have also become increasingly split along partisan lines, with sentiment swinging depending on which party holds the White House. Both factors have led some economists to discount the survey’s signal.

Sentiment data don’t always line up with actual spending, and consumers who say they’re gloomy often keep spending. Still, the report offers a timely read on how households are processing inflation, tariffs, the job market and stock prices. The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index, released later in the month, tends to place more weight on labor market conditions.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold breaks below $4,000 target area before bouncing. What do buyers need to prove?
item.description:
In yesterday’s educational post, I discussed why gold was falling despite sharply lower Treasury yields. Lower yields would typically provide support for a non-interest-bearing asset like gold. However, the dollar was mixed, and gold’s inability to reclaim its hourly moving averages kept the technical bias tilted toward the sellers. The fundamental expectation needed confirmation from the price action. It did not get it.

Today, that technical story continued with a break below $4,000 before buyers finally pushed back.

In today’s video, I walk through the chart, the sequence of breaks, and the levels that will help determine whether this rebound can develop into something more.

The moving averages told traders who was in control

Earlier this week (on Monday), gold fell back below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages (blue and green lines on the chart above) near $4,153 and stayed below.

That matters. When the price is below those moving averages, sellers have the stronger technical hand. A rally toward them gives buyers an opportunity to challenge that control, while giving sellers a level against which to define risk.

Yesterday, buyers had another shot. The rebound tested the moving-average resistance but could not sustain a break above it. The price rotated lower.

The sellers remained in control, and the next downside target came into focus.

Breaking $4,065.94 opened the door lower

The chart highlights repeated tests of support near $4,065.94 in the month of October including during the day yesterday. When that floor finally gave way, the selling accelerated.

The price moved through the $4,018.79 swing level, broke below the natural support at $4,000, and reached approximately $3,986 before bouncing.

This is why identifying targets ahead of time is useful. A break of support gives traders a reason to look toward the next area where buyers might respond. It also gives sellers a place to reassess after an extended move.

Today, buyers responded below $4,000 and pushed the price back above $4,018.79.

That is a constructive first step. There is still more work to do.

What needs to happen next?

For buyers, $4,018.79 becomes an initial barometer. Staying above that level would help the rebound build a base. The nearby $4,023.48 level is another hurdle, followed by the more important broken floor at $4,065.94.

Getting back above $4,065.94—and staying above—would take some of the pressure off and suggest the downside break is losing momentum.

Above that, the larger hurdles remain the falling hourly moving averages. On the supplied chart, those are approximately:

  • 100-hour moving average: $4,102.35

  • 200-hour moving average: $4,129.83

Until buyers reclaim those moving averages, sellers retain the stronger near-term technical position.

On the downside, a move back below $4,018.79 would put $4,000 and today’s low near $3,986 back in play. Below that low, the next swing support area comes between approximately $3,942.71 and $3,959.37.

Trade what the price is telling you

The rebound shows that buyers are willing to lean against lower levels. It does not yet establish that they have taken control.

For me, the process remains the same: define the bias, identify where that bias would be challenged, and know the next targets.

Sellers defended the moving averages. Support broke. Lower targets were reached. Now buyers have responded, and the technical levels give us a way to judge that response.

In today’s video, I take a closer look at those levels and what buyers need to do to turn a bounce into a stronger recovery.

---------------------------------------------------

My analysis is that Gold is falling. What are other's seeing?Where could XAUUSD go from here? Watch this week's Exness Trade of the Week for the key market factors and possible scenarios. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US S&P Global flash October services PMI 57.9 vs 58.0 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 59.8
  • Manufacturing 56.0 vs 55.5 expected
  • Prior manufacturing 57.0
  • Composite 57.6 vs 58.4 prior
  • selling prices rose at the sharpest rate since August 2022
  • New orders highest in over four-and-a-half years
  • Business output expectations for the 12 months ahead cooled compared to September but were still the second highest seen this year

One of the big surprises last month -- and one that the market took as a hawkish signal at time time -- was the jump in this survey. Employment was at the strongest since June 2022 and input cost inflation at the highest since Oct 2022.

Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence:

“October’s flash PMI data indicate that the US economy continues to boom at the start of the fourth quarter. The output readings from the survey are consistent with GDP growing at a 5% annualized rate after a 4% expansion was signalled for the third quarter. Especially healthy corporate earnings and profits are also indicated, and hiring has surged as companies seek to boost capacity to fulfil stronger customer demand.
“If the reopening of the economy after COVID is excluded, recent months have seen the best growth spell for US businesses since early 2015.
“However, cost pressures remain a key concern, notably as the renewed surge in oil prices reverberates through to impact a wide variety of goods and services. Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers. The result is the sharpest increase in selling prices for over four years to a pace that indicates consumer price inflation is likely to rise further above the Fed’s target in the coming months.”

If the Fed took this report seriously, they would be hiking next week. In theory, it's a good forward-looking indicator at the front edge of leading indicators but in practice, it's been mediocre at predicting economic momentum in the post-covid period.

For background, the S&P Global publishes flash estimates of its US Purchasing Managers’ Indexes for manufacturing and services each month at 9:45 am ET, usually about a week before the month ends. The flash readings are based on roughly 85% of survey responses, making them one of the earliest snapshots of US business conditions. Final figures follow in the first days of the next month and rarely differ much from the flash.

The indexes are diffusion measures built from surveys of purchasing managers at private-sector companies. A reading above 50 indicates expansion from the prior month and below 50 signals contraction. The manufacturing PMI is a composite of five sub-indexes: new orders, output, employment, suppliers’ delivery times and stocks of purchases. The services headline is the business activity index, based on a single question about activity levels. The two feed into a composite output index, which gives a broad read on private-sector growth.

The sub-indexes are often more revealing than the headlines. Input prices and output prices, or prices charged, offer an early gauge of cost pressures and how much firms are passing them on to customers, which makes them closely watched for inflation signals. Employment, new orders, export orders and business expectations add detail on demand and hiring.

The S&P Global PMIs tend to move markets less than the ISM surveys, which have a longer history and a larger following, though the two sometimes diverge. Their main advantage is timing and comparability. Flash PMIs for the eurozone, UK, Japan, Australia and India land the same day, giving traders a synchronized look at the global economy and letting them judge US momentum against other major economies.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD falls below 1.4000 as stronger Canadian spending keeps sellers in control
item.description:
Canadian consumers stepped up their spending in August. Statistics Canada reported retail sales increased 1.2% to $74.6 billion, with gains across all nine subsectors. The encouraging detail is that sales volumes also increased 1.2%. There was real buying behind the headline increase.

The strength extended beyond autos and gasoline. Core sales rose 1.1%, reversing July’s 0.7% decline, with food, general merchandise, and health and personal care retailers contributing. Gasoline was the exception to the volume story: receipts increased 1.7%, but volumes fell 0.5%, indicating higher prices drove that gain.

Quick analysis:

Today’s report gives the Canadian economy some better news, but the broader data are still telling a mixed story. The increase in retail volumes is encouraging after real gross domestic product was unchanged in July. It points to a stronger contribution from goods consumption in August, although retail spending is only one part of overall growth.

The employment picture is the concern. Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September, including 35,000 full-time positions, while unemployment increased to 6.5% from 6.4%. That was the second consecutive monthly employment decline. Consumers have continued spending, but sustained job losses would make that strength harder to maintain. Remember, the August retail figures predate September’s employment decline, while the September spending estimate is still preliminary.

Inflation also needs a look beneath the headline. September’s Consumer Price Index rose 3.1% year over year, up from 3.0%, largely because of gasoline. Excluding gasoline, inflation slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. Underlying measures eased as well: CPI-trim slipped to 1.8% from 1.9%, while CPI-median fell to 1.9% from 2.0%. Those measures help filter out unusually large price changes. The message is that higher energy costs are lifting headline inflation, while broader price pressures have moderated.

For the Bank of Canada, there are competing forces: resilient spending, weaker employment, and softer underlying inflation despite the energy-driven headline increase. The Bank held its policy rate at 2.25% in September, with its next decision and updated forecasts due October 28. My take is that today’s retail figures could reduce the urgency to ease, but they do not erase the employment concerns. The normal currency bias from stronger spending would support the Canadian dollar and pressure USDCAD lower, although the mixed economic backdrop makes a sustained move less clear-cut.

What are the price action and technicals telling traders?

Stronger Canadian spending would normally support the Canadian dollar and push USDCAD lower. That is what is happening, with the technicals reinforcing the downside bias.

Looking at the hourly chart, the price has fallen to a new session low at 1.3983, extending back below the natural support at 1.4000.

Earlier in the Asian-Pacific session, the pair dipped to 1.39963, but sellers could not sustain the break below 1.4000. The subsequent bounce took the price back toward the 50% midpoint of the move up from the August 21 low at 1.40149. The high reached 1.4018 before rotating back to the downside.

Buyers had their shot above the midpoint. They could not build on it. The reversal to fresh lows keeps sellers in control.

What comes next on the downside?

The next downside target is an older swing area between 1.3948 and 1.3966, which originated back in late March. Sellers would first need to break below the upper boundary at 1.3966, opening the door for a test of 1.3948.

The 61.8% retracement of the move up from the August low also sits near the lower boundary of that area. That adds to its importance as a potential support zone where buyers could lean and define their risk.

Back on September 16, when the Federal Reserve raised rates to 4.0%, the price surged above that swing area. The rally ultimately carried USDCAD to a double top at 1.42984, reached on October 9 and October 14.

A sustained break below 1.3948 and the nearby 61.8% retracement would give sellers another technical victory and shift attention toward the 200-day moving average at 1.38814.

Seven consecutive lower closes?

Since the second peak last Wednesday, USDCAD has closed lower for six consecutive trading days. Yesterday’s close was near 1.4005. Stay below that level into today’s close, and the losing streak would extend to seven.

The sellers have the momentum. Now they need to keep breaking—and staying below—the next downside targets.

What would hurt the downside momentum?

The first step for buyers would be a move back above the 50% midpoint at 1.40149. Getting above and staying above that level would take some of the immediate pressure off the pair.

Beyond that, buyers would need to work through two additional hurdles:

  • 100-day moving average at 1.40432
  • Falling 100-hour moving average at 1.4049

Those moving averages create an important resistance zone. A sustained move above both would disappoint sellers looking for more downside and give buyers a stronger technical foothold.

Until then, the failed bounce above the midpoint and the move to fresh lows keep the sellers in control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada August retail sales +1.2% vs +1.3% expected
item.description:
• The advance August reading was +1.3%
  • Prior was -0.7%
  • Sales up in all 9 subsectors, led by motor vehicles
  • Ex-autos +1.2% vs +1.0% expected
  • Prior ex-autos was -0.7%
  • September advance sales +0.7%

The advance (or flash) reading is the real market mover in this report now as it generally corresponds with the final reading. The +0.7% m/m number for September is a good sign of ongoing strength.

RBC last week was out with its cardholder spending data for September and that's usually a good cross-check and precursor to the official report. It showed core sales up 0.5% m/m on strong discretionary categories.

With that, the market should feel increasingly comfortable that the Bank of Canada will hike rates next week, as is priced at just under 80%. What's notable though is that Fed pricing has come down quickly so there is an interesting divergence opening up and -- not surprisingly -- USD/CAD is at a one-month low and broke 1.40 today.

The RBC data showed strong discretionary numbers and that showed up here as well with sales at food and beverage retailers up 1.1%. Furniture and appliances were also strong against a run of dismal housing numbers.

For background, Statistics Canada publishes its retail trade report monthly at 8:30 am ET, roughly seven weeks after the reference month ends. The release includes full data for that month plus an advance estimate for the following month, so each report gives markets two readings: a detailed look back and an early flash on the most recent month.

The headline figure is the monthly change in total retail sales in current dollars. Because car sales and gasoline prices can swing the total sharply, markets focus on core retail sales, which exclude motor vehicle and parts dealers and gasoline stations and fuel vendors. StatCan also reports sales in volume terms, stripping out price changes, which gives a better sense of how much consumers are actually buying. In periods of high inflation, nominal gains can mask flat or falling volumes.

The report breaks sales down across subsectors, including food and beverage retailers, general merchandise, health and personal care, building materials and garden equipment, clothing and furniture. It also tracks e-commerce sales and provincial results.

Retail sales are one of the more market-moving Canadian releases after jobs and CPI. A strong or weak print in core sales can shift Bank of Canada rate expectations and move the Canadian dollar, though the advance estimate often matters more than the stale full-month figure. The data also feed into monthly GDP estimates.

The report covers only goods sold through stores and online, so it misses spending on services such as travel, restaurants and entertainment. That makes it a partial gauge of consumer health. Its importance has grown as tariffs, higher prices and weaker sentiment test how much Canadian households can keep spending.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Tech selloff leaves buyers on the defensive
item.description:
The technology buyers had their shot on Wednesday. On Thursday, sellers took back control.

That is the backdrop heading into the final North American session of the week. U.S. stock futures are modestly lower after yesterday’s sharp declines in technology shares, Treasury yields are recovering some of their steep fall, and the Middle East headlines continue to keep the oil market on edge.

The dollar, however, is not moving in one direction against everything. It is higher against the EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and AUD, but marginally lower against the CAD and NZD. With U.S. business surveys and consumer sentiment still ahead, there is another opportunity for the data to give traders the next shove.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

Yesterday’s selloff: Technology takes the hit

Yesterday’s near-unchanged Dow did not tell the story underneath the surface. The selling was concentrated in technology and semiconductor shares, with the Nasdaq indices suffering the largest losses. The closing numbers were:

  • Dow industrial average: Up 11.98 points, or 0.02%, at 52,873.28.

  • S&P 500: Down 93.74 points, or 1.21%, at 7,663.43.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 694.00 points, or 2.60%, at 26,008.86.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 863.83 points, or 2.90%, at 28,958.69.

  • Russell 2000: Up 3.01 points, or 0.11%, at 2,784.03.

Investors continued to question whether the returns from the AI buildout would justify the spending involved. Semiconductor weakness added to the pressure, and market breadth was negative. On the Nasdaq, 1,734 stocks declined versus 1,471 advancing. The damage extended beyond just a few heavily weighted names.

Apple was the exception among the Magnificent Seven, closing higher while the other six declined. Meanwhile, the sharp fall in Treasury yields failed to provide the support that growth stocks would normally welcome. That combination tells you where the market’s attention was focused: earnings expectations, investment costs and whether future profits can justify current valuations.

For buyers, a lower price is only a starting point. What matters next is whether the price can recover broken technical levels and stay above them. Until that happens, a bounce can still be a correction within a move controlled by sellers.

For more background, see Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble.

This morning’s futures snapshot shows:

  • Dow futures: Down 31.4 points.

  • S&P 500 futures: Down 17 points.

  • Nasdaq 100 futures: Down 7.50 points.

Those are much smaller moves than yesterday’s cash-market declines. However, the buyers have yet to show much of a rebound.

The dollar is mixed, with the Swiss franc under pressure

The dollar’s largest gain is against the Swiss franc, with USDCHF up 0.46% near 0.8242. The greenback is also higher against sterling and the euro, with GBPUSD down 0.22% near 1.3370 and EURUSD down 0.20% near 1.1192.

Against the yen, the dollar is modestly higher, with USDJPY up 0.08% near 156.89. AUDUSD is down 0.06% near 0.7015.

The exceptions are the Canadian and New Zealand dollars. USDCAD is down 0.05% near 1.4001, while NZDUSD is up 0.02% near 0.5683. Those changes are small, but they reinforce the point that this is a mixed dollar market.

Currency ranges: There is still room to roam in several pairs

Using the displayed session highs and lows against the supplied 22-day average ranges, EURUSD has traded from 1.1185 to 1.1226. That is a 41-pip range, or about 63% of its 65-pip average. GBPUSD has traded from 1.3370 to 1.3407, a 37-pip range, or about 52% of its 71-pip average.

Both still have room to extend if the North American data provide a catalyst.

USDJPY has already done more traveling. Its range from 156.08 to 157.15 covers 107 pips, or about 111% of its 96-pip average. That does not prevent another extension, but it does mean the pair has already exceeded a normal day’s range.

USDCHF has also covered nearly a full average range, trading from 0.8193 to 0.8243—50 pips, or about 96% of its 52-pip average.

The quieter pairs have more unused range. USDCAD has traded from 1.3998 to 1.4021, covering 23 pips, or about 35% of its 66-pip average. AUDUSD’s 0.7005 to 0.7024 range is 19 pips, or about 41% of its 46-pip average. NZDUSD has traded from 0.5680 to 0.5699, also 19 pips, or about 46% of its 41-pip average.

USDCAD has the most room relative to its normal range, with Canadian retail sales still ahead. An average range is context, however. It is not a requirement that the market travel the remaining distance.

Treasury yields rebound after yesterday’s plunge

Treasury yields are moving higher this morning. The 2-year yield is at 4.6924%, up 5.74 basis points, while the 5-year is at 4.8210%, up 5.30 basis points. The 10-year is back near the 5% level at 4.9966%, up 4.36 basis points, and the 30-year is at 5.3092%, up 2.22 basis points.

The move follows yesterday’s decline of roughly 15–19 basis points across those maturities.

The question today is whether the data support that move lower in yields or encourage more of a retracement higher. The growth readings will matter, but so will the inflation details.

Middle East risks keep oil in focus

The supplied overnight headlines offer little comfort for traders looking for a quick resolution to the Iran conflict.

According to the Financial Times report cited in the news feed, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said the U.S. was prepared for a prolonged standoff with Iran and acknowledged that the stalemate could persist a year from now.

Separately, Fox News reported that Iran’s IRGC threatened to target U.S. bases if commercial ships continued transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The feed also carried a Sabereen report of a missile launch by Yemeni armed forces toward Saudi interests. That remains an attributed report.

Against that backdrop, the supplied update showed December WTI reaching a fresh session high of $101.19.

The market keeps looking for a diplomatic breakthrough. In the meantime, threats to shipping and regional energy infrastructure keep supply risks in the price. Higher oil also complicates the inflation outlook just as investors are questioning parts of the growth story.

Gold breaks $4,000, while copper gives sellers a technical opening

Gold fell back below the $4,000 level, reaching $3,986.85, before bouncing (see post here).

The bounce shows that buyers responded below the round number. What matters next is whether they can sustain a recovery above $4,000. A brief move back above followed by another failure would leave the rebound vulnerable. Getting above and staying above would give buyers a better foothold.

Copper has also reached an important decision point. The price fell below its 100-hour moving average at $6.449.

That moving average now gives traders a level to lean against. Stay below is more bearish and gives sellers some control in the short term. If sellers can maintain that break, the 200-hour moving average at $6.226 becomes the next downside target.

Conversely, a move back above $6.449—and the ability to stay above—would weaken the sellers’ case. Sellers have made a play. Now they need to hold the break.

European data point to uneven growth

The European flash PMI readings were mixed, but the broader euro-area results fell short of expectations.

France was the weak spot. Manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 versus 50.5 expected, while services dropped to 48.4 versus 50.7 expected. Both readings are below 50, indicating contraction.

Germany’s manufacturing sector held up better, with a reading of 54.2 versus 53.5 expected, but services missed at 51.7 versus 52.5 expected.

For the euro area overall, manufacturing came in at 52.4 versus 52.7 expected, while services registered 51.7 versus 52.6 expected. Those readings still indicate expansion, but at a slower pace than anticipated.

European equities are also lower in the supplied snapshot:

  • Germany’s DAX: Down 0.75%.

  • France’s CAC 40: Down 0.70%.

  • U.K. FTSE 100: Down 0.50%.

  • Spain’s IBEX: Down 0.20%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: Down 0.42%.

North American calendar: Growth and inflation expectations

At 8:30 AM ET, Canadian retail sales are expected to rise 1.3%, following a 0.7% decline. Sales excluding autos are expected to increase 1.1%, also following a 0.7% decline. With USDCAD’s range still relatively narrow, the report could provide a catalyst for an extension.

At 9:45 AM ET, the U.S. flash PMIs will provide an early look at October business conditions. Manufacturing is expected at 55.4 versus 55.9 previously, while services are expected at 57.9 versus 58.8. Both forecasts remain comfortably above 50. Traders will also be looking at what businesses say about prices, hiring and new orders.

At 10:00 AM ET, the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading is expected to remain at 46.3. The supplied calendar shows the previous one-year inflation expectations reading at 4.7%. With oil elevated, the inflation expectations details deserve attention alongside the headline sentiment number.

EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD: Define the risk before the next move

EURUSD is trading closer to the bottom of its overnight range, with 1.1185 the session low and 1.1226 the high. Sellers have the intraday directional advantage, but a break below the low would need follow-through. A failed break would give buyers an opening to push back into the range.

USDJPY has already exceeded its average daily range. The 156.08 low and 157.15 high frame the session so far. After that amount of movement, I want the technical levels to define the risk. Chasing a move without a nearby level to lean against makes managing that risk more difficult.

GBPUSD is trading at the bottom of its displayed range near 1.3370, with 1.3407 the session high. Sellers are pressing, and the pair still has room relative to its average range. Holding below the low would support an extension. Failure to stay below would take some of the immediate pressure off.

In the video, I work through the technical tools applied to the price action for each pair. The goal is to define who has control, what would change that control and where the next targets lie.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
item.description:
Rate hikes by year-end

  • RBNZ: 38 bps (99% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 109 bps

  • BoE: 37 bps (97% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 114 bps

  • BoC: 31 bps (78% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 97 bps

  • RBA: 20 bps (60% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 29 bps

  • Fed: 23 bps (92% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 67 bps

  • ECB: 18 bps (92% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 67 bps

  • BoJ: 14 bps (98% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 80 bps

  • SNB: 5 bps (82% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 53 bps

  • Last week's market pricing here. The 2027 pricing indicates the total amount of tigthening expected by the end of 2027, not how much is expected in 2027 alone.

We've got a hawkish repricing in near-term interest rate expectations for the RBA, BoC and the BoE after economic data and central bank speakers. The probabilities for an RBA rate hike at the upcoming meeting increased after RBA's Hauser delivered some hawkish comments that suggested a rate hike could come in November. He said the inflation outlook looks worse than forecast, the quarterly trimmed mean is likely to exceed expectations and capacity pressures are more elevated than assumed. He also added that forecasts are still being finalised and he does not know for sure what the Board will decide, which is why the probabilities stand around 60% and not higher.

For the BoC, the expectations for a rate hike increased after BoC Governor Macklem said the Bank would have to assess whether inflation would return to target on its own or whether it would need to raise interest rates to bring inflation down. That was a more direct tightening signal than the previous message of the Bank just monitoring inflation. Macklem said the risk of persistently high oil spreading beyond energy into the prices of other goods and services making inflation more persistent had increased. For context, underlying inflation has been moving lower in Canada, with the latest Trimmed-Mean CPI Y/Y falling to 1.8%, the lowest since 2020. I think a rate hike would be the wrong move considering the US-Canada trade war and softening labour market. 

For the BoE, the data this week reinforced expectations for a rate hike at the November meeting. Wage growth was stronger than expected, with regular pay rising 3.7% y/y versus 3.6% expected. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.7% versus 5.0% expected, with 102K jobs gained in the three months to August versus 5K expected. September CPI accelerated to 3.5% from 3.1%, above the 3.4% consensus. Core CPI also increased, rising to 2.8% from 2.6%, while services inflation climbed to 3.7% from 3.4%. Finally, the composite PMI rose to 53.1 from 52.0, its highest since February, beating expectations. Business activity, new orders and employment improved, while input-cost inflation accelerated to its highest level since June, reinforcing concerns that energy-driven price pressures could become more persistent amid resilient economic activity.

On the ECB side, we've got some dovish repricing as growth concerns increased amid bond market woes, increasing energy prices and ECB tightening. Today, we got the Flash PMIs for the major Eurozone economies and the data confirmed that economic activity has slowed and the expectations for the coming months have deteriorated. 

Finally, on the Federal Reserve side we've seen some notable dovish repricing as market's focus shifted from inflation fears to growth concerns amid prolonged Middle East crisis, widening credit spreads and persistent inflationary pressures that force the Fed to tighten monetary conditions. The losses in the stock market have also been a major driver of the dovish repricing as an AI-bubble burst would have huge negative wealth effect. We still have the US PMIs today that could change interest rate expectations, so it's going to be an important catalyst. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Zcash falls sharply as intensifying growth concerns weigh on the crypto market

The report also indicated that US was reinforcing its military presence in the region, with additional forces expected to be fully deployed by early November.

The risk of another direct confrontation between the US and Iran, combined with growing concerns about economic growth and the Federal Reserve forced to keep a hawkish stance due to inflationary pressures, weighed heavily on the crypto market.

item.title: Macro pulse: Europe's economy is losing steam but inflation won't let up
item.description:
The latest October PMI readings today don't paint a particularly encouraging picture of the health of the euro area economy. Growth is slowing and businesses are feeling the pinch, but inflation pressures are still refusing to go away. And that is the sort of headache that the ECB really doesn't need right now.

The data showed disappointing readings from both the manufacturing and services sectors, with the latter slowing rather markedly. A lot of that can be attributed to France though, as business activity there returned to contraction in October. And while Germany continues to hold up better, the broader slowdown across the region is becoming more difficult to ignore as we look to the final quarter this year.

With that in mind, this is where things get uncomfortable for the ECB. While business activity are showing signs of slowing down, price pressures haven't quite followed suit.

In looking at the chart above, businesses are still grappling with elevated cost pressures. The report noted that manufacturers saw a sharp acceleration in input prices in October, largely driven by higher energy costs, with the latest increase being the steepest since May.

The only consolation to this is that output price inflation did at least ease a little on the month. However, that could also be hinting that businesses may be finding it harder to pass rising costs on to consumers.

So, that is all leaving the ECB with quite the dilemma.

Traders are pricing in roughly 90% odds that the ECB will leave rates unchanged at next week's meeting. But looking to December, traders are still assigning around 68% odds of a rate hike in the final month of the year.

As things stand, inflation pressures remain the most pressing concern for policymakers. But then, the data today also serves up a reminder that the euro area economy isn't exactly in the best of shape to withstand further tightening. In particular, France is the big name that is struggling the most amid fiscal worries and concerns surrounding public finances. And the risk of spillover effects to the rest of the region should not be discounted.

Taking that into consideration, the big question isn't so much whether the ECB will hold next week. That's pretty much a done deal. Instead, it is whether policymakers can afford to keep raising rates if growth continues to lose momentum while higher energy costs squeeze businesses and households alongside growing fiscal worries across the region.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil extends gains as Saudi-Houthi conflict and concerns of US-Iran attacks keep the market supported
item.description:
The bullish momentum in crude oil has been slowly picking up after The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed plans for renewed strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections, with additional forces expected to be fully deployed by early November.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict, meanwhile, continues with the Houthis recently targeting Saudi airports and energy infrastructure, including a reported strike near Dammam that killed two people and injured eight. Saudi Aramco instructed staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following the latest security incidents.

The attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have intensified recently after Iran said in early October that it would close illegal routes used by the US to escort vessels through the strait. The IRGC claimed yesterday that it attacked four vessels and three others struck naval mines. This morning, Iran claimed that the illicit vessel traffic in Hormuz stopped after the continued attacks.

Looking ahead, crude oil remains supported amid the tensions in the Middle East and the prospects of another US attack against Iran after the midterms. Unless we get a de-escalation in the Saudi-Houthi conflict or a surprising breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations, oil prices will likely continue to rise.  

 

CRUDE OIL TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that crude oil(CFD contract) is slowly edging higher as prospects of another US attack on Iran is increasing the risk premium. If we get a pullback into the 96.77 zone, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the level, to keep targeting the 110.00 resistance. If the price gets there, we can expect the sellers to step in, with a defined risk above the resistance, to position for a drop back into the lower bound of the channel.

The buyers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

item.title: Bitcoin erases all the weekly gains as growth concerns lead to widespread risk aversion. What's next?
item.description:
Bitcoin erased all the weekly gains in the past couple of days as widespread risk aversion weighed on the crypto market. The risk-off flows started late Wednesday following reports that the US military was reducing its troop presence at bases in the Middle East, while the State Department ordered staff cuts at diplomatic posts amid rising security risks and the possibility of renewed military action against Iran.

The selling pressure then intensified after The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed detailed plans for potential strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections. The report also said that the US was building up its military presence which is expected to be fully deployed by early November.

The prospects of another direct conflict between the US and Iran amid increasing growth concerns and a hawkish Fed are all strong bearish drivers for the crypto market.

The focus today will be on the US Flash PMIs as it could be another major catalyst given the growth concerns.  Weaker-than-expected data could intensify growth fears, weigh further on risk sentiment and trigger another selloff in Bitcoin. item.title: Gold gets caught in market liquidation despite falling real yields supporting higher prices
item.description:
Gold extended the losses yesterday after breaking below the 4,070 support as widespread risk aversion tightened financial conditions. It looks like gold have been driven mainly by liquidations to cover losses in the stock market, much like what we’ve seen in 2025.  

To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly.

The main drivers like real yields have been actually pointing to higher gold prices. In fact, real yields fell significantly as inflation expectations remain roughly unchanged given the increase in oil prices, while nominal Treasury yields fell due to growth concerns. This might be an opportunity for the buyers to fade the weakness and enter at better prices.

Today, the focus will be on the US Flash PMIs. If the data surprises to the downside, growth concerns will likely intensify, and we should get another dovish repricing. In this scenario, gold should be supported as real yields would fall further. Stronger than expected data, on the other hand, could quell growth fears in the near-term and put renewed pressure on gold.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) extended the losses yesterday after breaking below the 4,070 support. We are approaching a key support zone around the 3,885 level where we have also a major upward trendline for confluence. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the trendline, to position for a rally into new record highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to increase the bearish bets into the 3,500 level next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we can see more clearly the selloff after the price broke below the 4,070 support as more sellers piled in to target the 3,885 level. If we get a pullback before that, we can expect the sellers to step in again around the 4,070 resistance, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to extend the pullback into the downward trendline next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into the 3,885 support. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to pile in for a pullback into the major downward trendline, with the 4,070 resistance as the first target. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Todaywe conclude the week with the US Flash PMIs.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Eurozone October PMI misses estimates as growth slows, keeping ECB rate hike dilemma alive
item.description:
• Eurozone October flash services PMI 51.7 vs 52.5 expected
  • Prior 53.0
  • Eurozone October flash manufacturing PMI 52.4 vs 52.7 expected
  • Prior 52.9
  • Eurozone October flash composite PMI 51.9 vs 52.7 expected
  • Prior 53.1

After the softer prints from France and Germany, the weaker-than-expected results for the overall euro area are not all too surprising. But at least for now, business activity continues to grow with both output and new orders increasing for the fourth successive month in October, albeit at the slowest pace during this sequence.

A key drag on growth was a renewed drop in business activity in the French services sector. But there were also signs of weakness elsewhere in the region as growth also edged lower in the rest of the euro area for both the manufacturing and services sectors.

Looking to prices, manufacturers reported a sharp and accelerated increase in input prices in October amid higher energy costs mostly. The latest rise was the steepest since May and above the average for the year-to-date. However, the rate of output price inflation slowed in October at least with both Germany and France posting weaker increases in selling prices than in September. As for the rest of the euro area, they saw the rate of inflation accelerate as a whole.

Overall, the data pretty much underscores that higher interest rates are also starting to take a toll and dampening demand. But the picture of sustained growth and more stubborn inflation pressures will likely add to speculation of more aggressive policy tightening from the ECB down the road.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: Stocks slip as weak French PMI adds to economic worries
item.description:
• Eurostoxx -0.3%
  • Germany DAX -0.5%
  • France CAC 40 -0.6%
  • UK FTSE -0.2%
  • Spain IBEX -0.1%
  • Italy FTSE MIB flat

European indices are opening slightly lower across the board as the more cautious risk mood carries over from yesterday. The selling pressure isn't quite as intense for now, but there's little reason for investors to be feeling too optimistic either.

The selloff in Wall Street yesterday continues to cast a shadow over broader sentiment, with concerns surrounding AI-related stocks and elevated oil prices keeping investors on edge. US futures are also looking more tepid today, with S&P 500 futures down 0.1% for the time being.

And to kick start the session, economic data isn't offering much comfort either. France's October flash PMI figures were a notable disappointment, with the composite reading falling to 48.4 from 51.1 in September. That puts the French private sector back into contraction, as both manufacturing and services activity deteriorated amid weakening demand and heightened political uncertainty.

That being said, I wouldn't read too much into the French numbers alone just yet. Germany and the Eurozone PMI releases are still to come, and those will offer a better indication of whether the slowdown is spreading more widely.

For European stocks though, the concern is that weakening growth prospects are now adding to an already uncomfortable backdrop of higher bond yields, fiscal uncertainty, and a more fragile global risk sentiment.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
